The mobilization of cultural repertoires as interpretive support <1>is not ornament and comes close to</1> the field of <2>Law and Humanities</2> as described by Maria Paola Mittica <3>(2015, p. 25)</3>, Doctor in Sociology and Associate Professor at the <4>Università degli Studi di Urbino</4>, who proposes a structural distinction between <5>Law and Humanities</5>, “Law and Literature” and “Law and Music”, in which the first functions as “genus” and the others as “species”, alongside other cuts such as “Law and Film” and “Law and Art”. In this frame, the dialogue with the humanities does not shift the axis of validation of the argument to the aesthetic plane, since the methodological proposal is precisely to promote a controlled exchange between specialized competences, oriented toward building analytical instruments adequate to the object. Mittica summarizes the question by stating that, in <6>Law </6> <7>and Humanities</7>, “a research methodology is assumed that is intended to promote dialogue between different specialized competences” <8>Mittica</8><9>(Mittica, 2015, p. 25)</9>. Thus, the epigraphic use can be understood as a hermeneutic frame and a symptomatic record of the symbolic field, without needing to enter the evidentiary chain or replace dogmatic description, qualification and critique. <10>↩</10>

For the author, technofeudalism, a concept popularized by the French economist <1>Cédric Durand in</1> his work <2>Techno-</2><3>féodalisme: Critique de l'économie numérique </3>("Technofeudalism: Critique of the digital economy", in our translation), emerges as a paradigm capable of redefining our understanding of the bases of the global socioeconomic system, representing not only a transition of capitalism, but a structural rupture with its fundamental principles. Varoufakis <4>(2024, p. 207-208)</4> mentions Cédric Durand's book as one of the works that contributed substantially to the debate on the impact of big technology companies. In this sense, the author recognizes that Durand and the American Shoshana Zuboff, PhD in Social Psychology from <5>Harvard</5> <6>University</6>, professor emerita at <7>Harvard Business School</7> and author of the book “The age of surveillance capitalism: the fight for a human future at the new frontier of power” (“A era do capitalismo da vigilância”, in the Brazilian edition), helped intensify discussions on the power of the so-called Big Techs. Thus, Varoufakis agrees with Durand's and Zuboff's critique of surveillance capitalism's use of mechanisms of massive data collection to strengthen the monopoly of the technology giants. However, Varoufakis argues that Durand's and Zuboff's analysis does not go deep enough, believing that the problem in question lies beyond the mere increase in the market power of such companies. Thus, Varoufakis's divergence lies in the emphasis on the total transformation of the economic system itself. <8>↩</8>

The contribution of Ana Flávia Merino Lesnovski, expressed in her doctoral thesis entitled <1>Uma experiência </1> <2>paradigmática: jogos e tensões no encontro entre a narrativa e a interatividade em forma audiovisual e eletrônica</2>, defended before the Graduate Program in Social Communication of PUC-RS in 2014, is useful here not because its object is the regulation of platforms in a legal key, but because her thesis offers a particularly fertile conceptual grammar for understanding interactive experiences structured by technical control. <3>The author</3> argues that interactive narrative should be read neither as full freedom of the interactor, nor as pure deceit, but as a field of tensions in which text, system and participant are articulated in variable relations of choice, control, illusion, simulation, action and identity <4>Lesnovski</4><5>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7)</5>. Her argument is especially relevant in stating that the interactive experience creates a “controlled freedom”, in which the user's action occurs within a structure that foresees him and offers him margins of intervention without ever abandoning command over the conditions of possibility of the experience itself <6>Lesnovski</6><7>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 7; p. 18)</7>. In this key, the interactor is not a mere passive spectator, but neither is he sovereign over the environment: he acts within a system that anticipates possible positions, responses and paths. The author also examines the function of systems of reward and punishment as forms of control by the computational system over free and potentially uncontrolled actions of the interactor, observing that such mechanisms serve not only to reward or punish occasionally, but to keep the experience in flow, avoid excessive deviations and lead the interaction back to tracks intelligible to the system itself <8>Lesnovski</8><9>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 79-80)</9>. When there is imbalance, however, the experience itself may degenerate into frustration or punishment, which reveals the delicacy of the arrangement between felt freedom and structural limitation <10>Lesnovski</10><11>(Lesnovski, 2014, p. 175)</11>. For this thesis, this formulation matters because it makes it possible to describe platform architecture as a regime of practical organization of action, in which choices, rewards, frictions, visibilities and sanctions are not peripheral elements, but parts of one and the same technical-informational frame that distributes probabilities, conditions trajectories and produces legibility of the environment for purposes of governance. <12>↩</12>

The official “Patch Notes” channel functions as the recurring public record of changes to the game, organized in periodic entries, by patch, with titles and dates <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2>. The format is useful for general information and for minimal communicative transparency, but it is not designed as a tool of comparative auditability for the consumer who needs to reconstruct, technically, a before and after of a specific cosmetic, with objective parameters of demonstration. For dogmatics, the consequence is simple. In a regime in which the supplier can update continuously and even automatically, auditability cannot depend on whether the consumer happened to archive evidence or has the technical knowledge to produce handmade comparisons. If the system does not deliver, as a standard, sufficient comparative elements, controlling functional downgrading requires either clearer public criteria for change or <3>recomposition mechanisms as automated as the alteration</3> that dispense with impossible proof when the impact is relevant. <4>↩</4>

<1>Filomeno treats</1> the consumer's vulnerability as a structural presupposition of consumer-law protection. The author observes that, for evident reasons, among them the consumer's absolute lack of control over the products and services placed on the market and the absolute disproportion between their bargaining power and that of suppliers, one starts from the presupposition that the consumer is the vulnerable party in the consumer relationship, which justifies unequal legal treatment between naturally unequal parties and direct protective governmental action <2>Filomeno</2><3>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 61])</3>. The application of the CDC is not explained by classificatory formalism, but by a material finding of structural fragility that calls for normative correction. This vulnerability, moreover, is not reduced to possible economic insufficiency. Filomeno describes it as the consumer's fragility before the supplier also in informational and technical aspects, that is, with regard both to purchasing power and to the information made available and the specialized knowledge held by the supplier itself <4>Filomeno</4><5>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 61])</5>. For that very reason, the recognition of this vulnerability has a direct impact on contractual dogmatics: as the author notes, the finding that the consumer is the vulnerable party in consumer relationships causes the classical dogmas of full autonomy of the will, abstract equality and contractual intangibility to yield, precisely because such principles would only hold in full if the parties had equal real power of decision <6>Filomeno</6><7>(Filomeno, 2018, [p. 346])</7>. Consumer-law protection is already born, in its classical basis, founded on vulnerability as a structural datum of the relationship and not as an episodic exception. <8>↩</8>

In this sense, Wada (<1>2016</1>) helps show that informational inadequacy, in consumer law, is not reduced to the simple absence of data. The failure may also arise when the supplier ensures only formal access to information, but does so under conditions that frustrate its practical intelligibility. The problem, then, is not only omission, but communication that is materially insufficient, through excess, dispersion, complexity or little concrete usefulness. Along these lines, the author expressly states that “it is not enough to ensure formal access to information”, and that it must have the legally required attributes of “correctness, clarity, precision and conspicuousness” <2>Wada</2><3>(Wada, 2016, p. 207)</3>. The requirement is qualitative, not merely quantitative. Seen this way, informational noise also makes the consumer vulnerable. Information must be “precise (= neither prolix nor scarce)”, precisely so that it remains comprehensible and serviceable to the consumer's decision-making <4>Wada</4><5>(Marques apud Wada, 2016, p. 207)</5>. The author further observes that the supplier may not interfere “significantly and negatively with the consumer's capacity to understand the terms or conditions” of the contract, nor set up “barriers or difficulties” to understanding <6>Wada</6><7>(Wada, 2016, p. 142)</7>. Hence the relevance of treating semiotic vulnerability as a contemporary form of factual vulnerability: not because the consumer is psychologically weak, but because they may be exposed to communicational architectures that appear transparent while producing material opacity. <8>↩</8>
